label: Psychology
title: Why We Can't Walk Away – The Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: Why do we sit through a film we dislike, finish a book we stopped enjoying, or stay on a path long after it stopped fitting? In this calm video essay we look at Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer's theater ticket study, Barry Staw's research on escalating commitment, and why letting go can feel like admitting defeat. With the Stoic Epictetus, we ask what is still in our power – and why the past, however much it cost, is not.

sections.text:
You have paid for a ticket. The evening comes, it is raining, you are tired, and you no longer want to go. But you go anyway. Because you paid.

Or you are halfway through a book you are not enjoying. Two hundred pages in. Stopping now feels like wasting the two hundred pages you have already read.

It sounds reasonable. It even feels a little like a virtue. And yet psychologists and economists have a name for it, and it is not a compliment.

It is called the sunk cost fallacy. And once you see it, you may notice how many of your days are quietly shaped by things you can no longer change.

sections.heading: The Theater Tickets
sections.text:
In the early 1980s, the psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer ran a simple experiment at the Ohio University Theater.

At the start of the season, people came to the ticket booth to buy a season subscription. The normal price was fifteen dollars. But the researchers had arranged for some customers, chosen at random, to receive a discount. Roughly a third paid the full fifteen dollars. Another third paid thirteen. The last third paid only eight.

The plays were the same. The seats were the same. The only difference was how much each person had already spent.

Then the researchers simply counted who came. Over the following months, the people who had paid the full price attended more plays than those who had received a discount.

Think about what that means. Once the ticket is bought, the money is gone, whatever you do. The only real question left is whether tonight's play is worth your evening. But the people who had paid more seemed to feel they had to get their money's worth. A past purchase was steering present choices.

In the same paper, published in 1985, Arkes and Blumer asked students to imagine they had bought two ski trips for the same weekend by mistake. One to Michigan for a hundred dollars. One to Wisconsin for fifty, which they expected to enjoy more. Neither could be refunded. More than half chose Michigan. The more expensive trip. The one they expected to enjoy less.

sections.heading: Why Letting Go Feels Like Losing
sections.text:
Why would anyone choose the weekend they expect to enjoy less?

Part of the answer seems to be that we dislike waste. Arkes and Blumer suggested that people keep going partly so that they do not appear wasteful, to others and to themselves.

Another part has to do with how we feel about losses. In their work on prospect theory, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that losses tend to weigh more heavily than gains of the same size. As long as we keep going, the money or the years are not quite lost yet. They are an investment that might still pay off. The moment we stop, the loss becomes real, and we have to look at it.

And that may be the deepest part. Stopping can feel like a confession. I was wrong. I chose badly. All of that was for nothing.

So we keep going. Not because the future looks good, but because the past feels too painful to write off.

sections.heading: Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy
sections.text:
In 1976, the organizational psychologist Barry Staw published a study with a memorable title: Knee-deep in the big muddy.

He asked business students to play the role of a manager in a simulated company. First they had to decide which of two divisions should receive extra research money. Then they learned how that division had performed. For some, it had gone well. For others, it had gone badly. After that, they could divide a second, larger budget.

The striking result: the students who were personally responsible for a decision that had turned out badly tended to put more money into that same failing division, not less. This pattern became known as escalation of commitment.

Staw's interpretation was that people were trying to justify their earlier choice. Pulling out would mean admitting that the first decision had been a mistake. Investing more kept alive the hope that it might still be proven right.

A note of caution belongs here. Later attempts to repeat this exact experiment have had mixed results, and the size of the effect varies a lot from situation to situation. But the idea has stayed influential, because it describes something many people recognise. The harder we have fought for a decision, the harder it becomes to let it go.

sections.heading: What Is No Longer Ours

quote.lead: Nearly two thousand years ago, the Stoic teacher Epictetus gave his students a distinction that sounds almost too simple. The handbook of his teaching, collected by his student Arrian, opens with it:
quote.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
quote.author: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 – transl. George Long (1877)

sections.text:
For the Stoics, this was the starting point of a calm life. Our own judgments, choices and intentions are in our power. Much else is not: our bodies, our reputation, the actions of other people.

And the past may be the clearest example of all. What has been paid has been paid. The years spent on a project, the money spent on a ticket, the effort put into a plan that no longer fits. None of it can be changed by any decision we make tonight.

Seen this way, the sunk cost fallacy is a confusion about what is in our power. We act as if we could still rescue the past, as if going to the play could somehow bring back the money. But the money already belongs to the things that are not in our power. The only thing still within reach is the next choice.

A little later in the same handbook, Epictetus suggests that we never say about anything that we have lost it, but rather that we have given it back. He applies this to far greater losses than tickets. But the thought fits here too. What is gone is no longer ours to manage.

sections.heading: Looking Forward Instead
sections.text:
None of this means we should give up whenever things get hard. Persistence matters. Many good things, from learning an instrument to a long friendship, include stretches that feel like poor investments at the time.

The difference lies in the reason. Persistence looks forward: I continue because I still believe in where this is going. The sunk cost fallacy looks backward: I continue because of what I have already put in.

One simple question can help to tell them apart. Imagine you were starting from this exact point today, with nothing invested. Knowing what you know now, would you choose this? Would you buy this ticket tonight? Would you start this book on page two hundred?

If the answer is yes, go on, and go on gladly. If the answer is no, what you have already spent is not, on its own, a reason to stay.

Another small habit is to decide on a checkpoint before you begin. How much time or money am I willing to give this before I look at it again? A limit set calmly in advance is easier to respect than one set in the middle of a loss.

And when you do let something go, it can help to name what it gave you. The plays you did see. The things the project taught you. Letting go of a path does not erase what happened on it.

sections.heading: The Freedom of Now
sections.text:
There is something almost tender about the sunk cost fallacy. It comes from a wish to honour what we have given. Our money, our time, our effort, sometimes years of our lives. We do not want any of it to have been in vain.

But the past cannot be honoured by obeying it. What we have spent is already spent, and no future choice can bring it back or make it count twice.

The ticket is paid for either way. The only question left is how you want to spend this evening.

That is the quiet freedom hidden in this idea. Every morning, the past hands us a long list of reasons to keep doing what we have always done. Some of those reasons are good. Some are only the echo of what we have already paid.

You are allowed to tell them apart. You are allowed to leave at the interval. Not because what came before did not matter, but because what comes next still can.

short.title: Why we can't walk away
short.hook: They paid more. So they stayed.
short.text:
At the start of a theater season, researchers quietly gave some ticket buyers a discount. Some paid fifteen dollars, some thirteen, some eight.

The plays were the same. But the people who had paid the full price came to more of them.

Psychologists call this the sunk cost effect. Once we have put money, time or effort into something, we keep going, even when the future no longer justifies it.

The Stoic Epictetus began his handbook with a simple line: of things some are in our power, and others are not.

The past is not. So ask yourself: if you were starting today, would you choose this?
